response.sql:
WITH per_order AS (
  SELECT orderslink,
         AVG(rebtotal) AS avg_rebtotal,
         AVG(feerate - rebrate) AS avg_net_rate
  FROM fees
  GROUP BY orderslink
),
bench AS (
  SELECT AVG(avg_net_rate) AS benchmark
  FROM per_order
),
above AS (
  SELECT p.avg_rebtotal, p.avg_net_rate, b.benchmark
  FROM per_order p
  CROSS JOIN bench b
  WHERE p.avg_net_rate > b.benchmark
)
SELECT AVG(avg_rebtotal) AS avg_of_avg_rebtotal,
       AVG(avg_net_rate) AS avg_of_avg_net_rate,
       AVG(avg_net_rate - benchmark) AS avg_excess_over_benchmark
FROM above;

assumptions.assumption: Each fee record's net rate is feerate - rebrate. A record missing either value yields a NULL net rate, which AVG skips. Per-order averages skip NULL rebtotal values the same way.
The NULL-orderslink records form one group, as GROUP BY produces, and that group counts once in the benchmark like any order.
An order whose net rates are all NULL has a NULL average net rate. It is left out of the benchmark and cannot exceed it, so it is not returned.
The query uses standard SQL with CTEs and AVG, which runs on PostgreSQL and SQLite.

alternatives.interpretation: Compute each order's net fee rate as the average fee rate minus the average rebate rate, not as the average of per-record differences. This differs only when NULLs are present, because a record with one missing value then still contributes its other rate.
alternatives.sql:
WITH per_order AS (
  SELECT orderslink,
         AVG(rebtotal) AS avg_rebtotal,
         AVG(feerate) - AVG(rebrate) AS avg_net_rate
  FROM fees
  GROUP BY orderslink
),
bench AS (
  SELECT AVG(avg_net_rate) AS benchmark
  FROM per_order
),
above AS (
  SELECT p.avg_rebtotal, p.avg_net_rate, b.benchmark
  FROM per_order p
  CROSS JOIN bench b
  WHERE p.avg_net_rate > b.benchmark
)
SELECT AVG(avg_rebtotal) AS avg_of_avg_rebtotal,
       AVG(avg_net_rate) AS avg_of_avg_net_rate,
       AVG(avg_net_rate - benchmark) AS avg_excess_over_benchmark
FROM above;
